question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

PUGNACIOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Belligerent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pugnacious (adjective) means eager or quick to argue, quarrel or fight; aggressively combative in manner. (लड़ाकू, कलहप्रिय)
◦ Example: The pugnacious speaker turned every discussion into a confrontation.

 

• Belligerent carries exactly this sense — hostile, aggressive and ready to fight. (युद्धप्रिय, आक्रामक)
◦ Example: His belligerent tone made negotiation impossible.

 

• Both words derive from Latin roots of fighting — pugnare (to fight, from pugnus, "fist") and bellum (war). Recognising the root is the fastest way to solve such questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Conciliatory (सुलह कराने वाला): intended to pacify or end a disagreement — the opposite of pugnacious.

 

• Option 2: Diffident (संकोची): lacking self-confidence, shy and hesitant.

 

• Option 3: Placid (शांत): calm, peaceful and not easily upset — also an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of pugnacious frequently asked in SSC: truculent, bellicose, combative, quarrelsome and contentious.

 

• Antonyms: peaceable, amiable, docile, pacific.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

A Pyrrhic victory
option_1: A victory won without any effort
option_2: A win achieved at a ruinously heavy cost
option_3: A defeat deliberately disguised as success
option_4: A triumph shared equally by both sides
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A win achieved at a ruinously heavy cost.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "A Pyrrhic victory" means a success gained at so great a cost that it is scarcely worth winning — the winner is left almost as damaged as the loser. (ऐसी जीत जो भारी क्षति की कीमत पर मिले)
◦ Example: The company won the lawsuit, but the legal expenses made it a Pyrrhic victory.

 

• The idiom comes from King Pyrrhus of Epirus, who defeated the Romans at Heraclea and Asculum but lost so much of his army that he is said to have remarked that another such victory would ruin him.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes an effortless win, for which the idiom would be "a walkover" or "a cakewalk".

 

• Option 3 is a misreading; a Pyrrhic victory is a genuine victory, not a disguised defeat.

 

• Option 4 describes a drawn or mutually beneficial outcome, not a costly win.

 

NOTE

 

• Other allusive idioms often asked in SSC: "Achilles' heel" (a fatal weakness), "Herculean task" (a task needing enormous effort), "Damocles' sword" (an ever-present danger) and "Hobson's choice" (no real choice at all).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

PARSIMONIOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Generous.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Parsimonious (adjective) means extremely unwilling to spend money or use resources; excessively stingy. (अत्यंत कंजूस)
◦ Example: The parsimonious landlord refused to repair even the leaking roof.

 

• Its true opposite is generous — willing to give freely, openhanded. (उदार, दानशील)
◦ Example: She was generous with both her time and her money.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Frugal (मितव्ययी): careful and economical in spending — a synonym, and note that it carries a positive shade, unlike parsimonious.

 

• Option 3: Miserly (कंजूस): hoarding money and hating to part with it — the closest synonym.

 

• Option 4: Thrifty (बचत करने वाला): using money and resources prudently — again a synonym, not an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• In antonym questions SSC often fills three of the four slots with near-synonyms of the given word. Identify the sense of the word first, then eliminate every option that agrees with it.

 

• Other antonyms of parsimonious: lavish, munificent, bountiful, prodigal, extravagant.

question: Identify the misspelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Accomodation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is "Accommodation" — a room, building or space in which somebody may live or stay; also an arrangement or compromise. (आवास, ठहरने की व्यवस्था)
◦ Example: The department arranged free accommodation for the candidates.

 

• Spelling key: AC + COM + MO + DA + TION — it takes double "c" and double "m". A useful memory aid: accommodation is large enough to hold two cots (cc) and two mattresses (mm).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Reconnaissance (टोह, पूर्व सर्वेक्षण) — correctly spelt; military observation of a region. Note the double "n" and double "s".

 

• Option 2: Bureaucracy (नौकरशाही) — correctly spelt; ends in "-cracy", not "-cracey".

 

• Option 4: Questionnaire (प्रश्नावली) — correctly spelt; note the double "n" before "-aire".

 

NOTE

 

• Other double-letter words repeatedly tested by SSC: occurrence, embarrassment, harassment, committee, millennium, possession and necessary (one "c", two "s").

question: Spot the correct spelling of the surgical procedure performed for the removal of the gall bladder.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Cholecystectomy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Cholecystectomy" is the surgical removal of the gall bladder, most commonly performed today by laparoscopy. (पित्ताशय निकालने की शल्य क्रिया)
◦ Example: The patient recovered within a week of the laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

 

• Break the word into its Greek roots: CHOLE (bile) + CYST (bladder, sac) + ECTOMY (surgical removal). Reading long medical terms root by root is the reliable method for such questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Cholycystectomy" — incorrect; the root is "chole", not "choly".

 

• Option 3: "Colecystectomy" — incorrect; the "h" after the initial "c" has been dropped.

 

• Option 4: "Cholecystectomie" — incorrect; the English suffix is "-ectomy", not the French "-ectomie".

 

NOTE

 

• The suffix "-ectomy" means removal (appendectomy, tonsillectomy, nephrectomy), "-otomy" means a surgical cut (tracheotomy), and "-oscopy" means visual examination (endoscopy, laparoscopy).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A speech or piece of writing in high praise of a person, especially one who has recently died'
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Eulogy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A eulogy is a formal speech or written tribute that praises someone highly, typically delivered at a funeral or memorial service. (प्रशंसापरक भाषण)
◦ Example: The Vice-Chancellor delivered a moving eulogy at the professor's memorial.

 

• The word comes from Greek eu (good, well) + logia (speech) — literally "good words". The same prefix appears in euphony (pleasant sound) and euphemism (a mild word used in place of a harsh one).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Elegy (शोकगीत): a poem of mourning for the dead. It laments rather than praises — the commonest distractor for eulogy.

 

• Option 2: Epitaph (समाधि-लेख): the short inscription written on a tombstone.

 

• Option 3: Epilogue (उपसंहार): the concluding section of a book, play or film.

 

NOTE

 

• Related one-word substitutes: Obituary (a published notice of a death with a short biography), Prologue (an introductory section), Panegyric (an elaborate public speech of praise) and Requiem (a mass or music for the dead).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The forensic evidence was ___ conclusive; the jury deliberated for three more days.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. hardly.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The clue lies in the second clause: if the jury had to deliberate for three more days, the evidence clearly was not conclusive. The blank therefore needs a negative adverb of degree.

 

• "Hardly" means scarcely, almost not at all. (बमुश्किल, लगभग नहीं)
◦ Example: The signal was hardly audible over the noise of the traffic.

 

• Note that hardly, scarcely, barely and seldom are already negative in meaning, so they are never used with another negative word such as not or no.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: utterly (पूर्णतः) — completely; it would mean the evidence was fully conclusive, contradicting the second clause.

 

• Option 3: decidedly (निश्चित रूप से) — definitely, unmistakably; again the opposite of the required sense.

 

• Option 4: wholly (पूरी तरह) — entirely; also contradicts the context.

 

NOTE

 

• In such filler questions, always read the clause after the semicolon or comma — SSC usually plants the deciding clue there rather than in the clause containing the blank.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The scheme was rolled out ___ considerable opposition from local traders.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. amid.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Amid" means in the middle of, surrounded by, in an atmosphere of. It is used before uncountable nouns and abstract situations — opposition, protest, uncertainty, controversy, applause. (के बीच, के माहौल में)
◦ Example: The bill was passed amid widespread protest.

 

• Here "opposition" is an abstract, uncountable noun, so amid is the only fitting preposition.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: among — used for more than two countable things or people (among the traders, not among opposition).

 

• Option 2: between — used when two parties or clearly separate items are involved (between the government and the traders).

 

• Option 4: towards — indicates direction or attitude, which the sentence does not require.

 

NOTE

 

• Quick rule: amid + uncountable/abstract (amid confusion), among + countable plural (among the students), between + two identifiable parties (between the two states).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

No sooner had the results been declared ___ the candidates began celebrating outside the centre.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. than.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "No sooner" is always followed by "than" — they form a fixed correlative pair used to show that one action followed another immediately. (जैसे ही ... वैसे ही)
◦ Example: No sooner had the bell rung than the students rushed out.

 

• Because the sentence opens with the negative expression "No sooner", the clause undergoes inversion — the auxiliary comes before the subject: No sooner had the results been declared... The given sentence already follows this rule correctly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: when — belongs with "Hardly / Scarcely / Barely", not with "no sooner". (Hardly had he arrived when it began to rain.)

 

• Option 2: then — an adverb of time, not a conjunction; it cannot join the two clauses.

 

• Option 4: that — used with "such / so" (so tired that he slept), not with "no sooner".

 

NOTE

 

• Learn these fixed pairs for SSC: No sooner … than, Hardly/Scarcely … when, Such … that, So … that, Not only … but also, Neither … nor, Either … or, Lest … should.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Neither the manager nor the technicians (1)/ was able to explain (2)/ why the machinery had failed (3)/ during the trial run. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error lies in subject–verb agreement. When two subjects are joined by "neither … nor" (or "either … or"), the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it — this is called the Proximity Rule.

 

• Here the nearer subject is "the technicians", which is plural, so the verb must be "were", not "was".

◦ Corrected sentence: Neither the manager nor the technicians were able to explain why the machinery had failed during the trial run.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — "Neither the manager nor the technicians" is a properly formed compound subject.

 

• Part (3) is correct — the past perfect "had failed" rightly shows an action completed before the explaining.

 

• Part (4) is correct — "during the trial run" is an appropriate prepositional phrase of time.

 

NOTE

 

• Reverse the order and the verb changes: Neither the technicians nor the manager was able to explain…

 

• But with "and" the subject is always plural: The manager and the technicians were unable to explain…

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The committee's principal contention, that fiscal decentralisation invariably improves service delivery, (1)/ rest on an assumption (2)/ which the accompanying data does little (3)/ to substantiate. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject of the sentence is the singular noun "contention", so the verb must be "rests", not "rest".

◦ Corrected sentence: The committee's principal contention, that fiscal decentralisation invariably improves service delivery, rests on an assumption which the accompanying data does little to substantiate.

 

• The long clause set off by commas — that fiscal decentralisation invariably improves service delivery — is an appositive. Words placed between the subject and its verb, whether an appositive or a phrase beginning with along with, as well as, together with, in addition to, never change the number of the subject.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — the possessive "committee's" and the appositive clause are properly punctuated with a pair of commas.

 

• Part (3) is correct — "data" is treated as a singular collective here, so "does" is acceptable in standard modern usage.

 

• Part (4) is correct — "to substantiate" correctly completes the phrase "does little to substantiate".

 

NOTE

 

• In long SSC sentences, always strip away the material between commas and read the bare subject with the verb. Here it reduces to "the contention rests", which exposes the error at once.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

The municipal board will have completed the drainage survey by December.
option_1: The drainage survey will be completed by the municipal board by December.
option_2: The drainage survey would have been completed by the municipal board by December.
option_3: The drainage survey will have been completed by the municipal board by December.
option_4: The drainage survey has been completed by the municipal board by December.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The drainage survey will have been completed by the municipal board by December.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Future Perfect Tense — structure: Subject + will have + V3.

 

• The passive of the future perfect is formed as: Object + will have been + V3 + by + Subject.

◦ Active: The municipal board will have completed the drainage survey by December.
◦ Passive: The drainage survey will have been completed by the municipal board by December.

 

• In the conversion the object ("the drainage survey") becomes the subject, the subject ("the municipal board") moves after "by", and the tense is faithfully retained.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses "will be completed" — that is the passive of the simple future, not the future perfect.

 

• Option 2 uses "would have been", which shifts the sentence into the conditional/past future, changing the meaning.

 

• Option 4 uses "has been completed" — the passive of the present perfect, which wrongly places the action in the past.

 

NOTE

 

• Passive forms of the future group: Simple Future → will be + V3; Future Perfect → will have been + V3. Future Continuous and Future Perfect Continuous have no passive form in normal use.

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

It had been decided by the committee that the tender would be cancelled.
option_1: The committee has decided to cancel the tender.
option_2: The committee had decided that the tender would be cancelled.
option_3: The tender was cancelled by the committee's decision.
option_4: The committee was deciding the cancellation of the tender.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The committee had decided that the tender would be cancelled.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence uses the impersonal passive pattern "It had been + V3 + by + agent + that …", which is common with verbs of thinking and deciding — decide, believe, report, suggest, expect.

 

• To make it active: drop the introductory "It", bring the agent after "by" to the front as the subject, and keep the that-clause unchanged.

◦ Passive: It had been decided by the committee that the tender would be cancelled.
◦ Active: The committee had decided that the tender would be cancelled.

 

• The tense of the main verb, past perfect ("had been decided" → "had decided"), must be preserved exactly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 changes the tense to the present perfect and replaces the that-clause with an infinitive, altering the structure.

 

• Option 3 is still passive ("was cancelled") and also changes the meaning — it states that the tender was cancelled, whereas the original only records a decision.

 

• Option 4 shifts to the past continuous, suggesting an incomplete action rather than a decision already taken.

 

NOTE

 

• The reverse conversion follows the same pattern: People say that he is honest → It is said that he is honest / He is said to be honest.

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homophone of the highlighted word.

 

The critic argued that the novel deserved a place in the literary canon.
option_1: The canon of the cathedral led the morning prayers.
option_2: Scholars still debate the canon of classical Sanskrit drama.
option_3: Canon law governed such disputes for centuries.
option_4: The museum displayed an eighteenth-century cannon on its lawn.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The museum displayed an eighteenth-century cannon on its lawn.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another but is spelt differently and has a different meaning. (समोच्चारित किंतु भिन्न वर्तनी वाला शब्द)

 

• Canon (one "n") means an accepted body of works, a general rule or principle, or a senior member of the clergy of a cathedral.

• Cannon (double "n") means a large mounted gun or piece of artillery. The two are pronounced alike, so "cannon" is the homophone required.

◦ Example: The old cannon still stands at the entrance of the fort.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 all reuse the same spelling "canon". They illustrate different meanings of one word — that makes them homonyms, not homophones.

 

• Option 1 uses canon as a cathedral clergyman; Option 2 as a body of accepted literary works; Option 3 as ecclesiastical law.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember the distinction: Homophone → same sound, different spelling (canon/cannon, principal/principle, stationary/stationery, complement/compliment). Homonym → same spelling and sound, different meaning (bank, bat, spring). Homograph → same spelling, possibly different sound (lead, tear, wind).

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Though solitude and loneliness are habitually treated as synonyms, they describe fundamentally opposed conditions of the mind. Loneliness is an involuntary deprivation — the ache of wanting company and finding none. Solitude, by contrast, is a chosen withdrawal, a deliberate act of self-companionship. The lonely person is diminished by absence; the solitary person is replenished by it. History's most original minds — poets, mathematicians, reformers — have almost invariably guarded intervals of solitude, recognising that the intellect requires unpeopled hours in which to consolidate what crowded ones have merely gathered.

 

Modern life, however, has made such hours difficult to secure. The very devices designed to abolish distance have also abolished stillness, ensuring that no moment need ever be spent alone with one's own thoughts. The result is a curious paradox: a generation more continuously connected than any before it reports unprecedented levels of loneliness. Connection, it appears, is not companionship, and stimulation is a poor substitute for reflection.

 

Solitude, moreover, is not idleness. It demands a certain courage, for it strips away the reassuring noise by which we ordinarily avoid self-examination. Those unaccustomed to it often mistake its initial discomfort for emptiness and hurry back to the crowd. Yet that discomfort is precisely the point: it is in unhurried aloneness that judgement matures, grievances lose their heat, and the difference between what we truly want and what we merely covet becomes visible. A society that cannot tolerate silence will produce citizens who are articulate but unreflective — forever speaking, seldom understanding.

 

According to the passage, what fundamentally distinguishes solitude from loneliness?
option_1: Solitude occurs in rural areas, whereas loneliness occurs in cities
option_2: Solitude is temporary, whereas loneliness is permanent
option_3: Solitude is chosen, whereas loneliness is involuntary
option_4: Solitude requires company, whereas loneliness does not
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Solitude is chosen, whereas loneliness is involuntary.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The distinction is stated directly in the opening paragraph: loneliness is described as an involuntary deprivation, while solitude is called a chosen withdrawal, a deliberate act of self-companionship.

 

• The author reinforces the contrast in the next line — the lonely person is diminished by absence, the solitary person is replenished by it. The determining factor is therefore choice, not duration or place.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 introduces a rural–urban distinction that the passage never makes.

 

• Option 2 brings in duration, which is not the basis of the author's contrast.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the passage — solitude is precisely the absence of company, deliberately chosen.

 

NOTE

 

• For direct-detail questions, locate the sentence in the passage that answers the question and match it word for word. Options that add information not present in the passage are always wrong, however reasonable they sound.

What does the author mean by the expression "unpeopled hours"?
option_4: Periods deliberately spent away from company
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Periods deliberately spent away from company.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The prefix "un-" negates, so "unpeopled" literally means without people. "Unpeopled hours" are therefore stretches of time spent alone.

 

• The context confirms this: the author says the intellect needs such hours "in which to consolidate what crowded ones have merely gathered" — setting unpeopled hours directly against crowded ones. Since the whole paragraph is about chosen solitude, the aloneness is deliberate.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is ruled out by the third paragraph, where the author states explicitly that solitude is not idleness.

 

• Option 2 describes the obstacle to such hours, discussed later in the passage — not the meaning of the phrase itself.

 

• Option 3 confuses "unpeopled" with sleeplessness; the passage says nothing about nights or insomnia.

 

NOTE

 

• For vocabulary-in-context questions, split the word into its parts (un + people + ed) and then check the surrounding sentence for a contrasting word — here, "crowded" — which usually confirms the sense.

According to the passage, why do many people retreat from solitude?
option_2: They lack the leisure to pursue it
option_3: They mistake its initial discomfort for emptiness
option_4: They believe it hampers professional success
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. They mistake its initial discomfort for emptiness.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The final paragraph states the reason plainly: those unaccustomed to solitude mistake its initial discomfort for emptiness and hurry back to the crowd.

 

• The author explains why the discomfort arises — solitude strips away the reassuring noise by which we ordinarily avoid self-examination, and facing oneself demands courage.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is not mentioned; the passage never says solitude carries a social stigma.

 

• Option 2 refers to the scarcity of quiet hours in modern life, which is a separate point in the second paragraph and not the reason people flee solitude.

 

• Option 4 introduces a career argument that appears nowhere in the passage.

 

NOTE

 

• SSC distractors in comprehension are usually of two kinds: statements that are true of the passage but answer a different question, and statements that are plausible in real life but absent from the passage. Options 2 and 4 illustrate the two types respectively.

option_1: Wise people are usually the least educated

The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The most continuously connected generation reports the highest loneliness.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The paradox is stated in the second paragraph: a generation more continuously connected than any before it reports unprecedented levels of loneliness.

 

• The author resolves it in the next sentence — connection is not companionship, and stimulation is a poor substitute for reflection. Devices meant to abolish distance have also abolished stillness.

 

• A paradox is a statement that seems self-contradictory yet expresses a truth. (विरोधाभास) Here, more contact producing more loneliness is exactly such a truth.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is not claimed anywhere in this passage.

 

• Option 2 is a play on words; the author speaks of society being unable to tolerate silence, not of silence becoming noisy.

 

• Option 4 reverses the author's argument — technology is presented as the obstacle to reflection.

 

NOTE

 

• When a question asks for a paradox, irony or contrast, look for signal words in the passage such as "however", "yet", "by contrast" and "the result is a curious paradox" — the answer is almost always in that very sentence.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Though solitude and loneliness are habitually treated as synonyms, they describe fundamentally opposed conditions of the mind. Loneliness is an involuntary deprivation — the ache of wanting company and finding none. Solitude, by contrast, is a chosen withdrawal, a deliberate act of self-companionship. The lonely person is diminished by absence; the solitary person is replenished by it. History's most original minds — poets, mathematicians, reformers — have almost invariably guarded intervals of solitude, recognising that the intellect requires unpeopled hours in which to consolidate what crowded ones have merely gathered.

 

Modern life, however, has made such hours difficult to secure. The very devices designed to abolish distance have also abolished stillness, ensuring that no moment need ever be spent alone with one's own thoughts. The result is a curious paradox: a generation more continuously connected than any before it reports unprecedented levels of loneliness. Connection, it appears, is not companionship, and stimulation is a poor substitute for reflection.

 

Solitude, moreover, is not idleness. It demands a certain courage, for it strips away the reassuring noise by which we ordinarily avoid self-examination. Those unaccustomed to it often mistake its initial discomfort for emptiness and hurry back to the crowd. Yet that discomfort is precisely the point: it is in unhurried aloneness that judgement matures, grievances lose their heat, and the difference between what we truly want and what we merely covet becomes visible. A society that cannot tolerate silence will produce citizens who are articulate but unreflective — forever speaking, seldom understanding.

 

What does the author warn about a society that cannot tolerate silence?
option_1: It will gradually lose its cultural heritage
option_2: It will produce citizens who speak much but reflect little
option_3: It will abandon formal education altogether
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It will produce citizens who speak much but reflect little.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage closes with the warning that such a society will produce citizens who are articulate but unreflective — forever speaking, seldom understanding.

 

• Articulate means fluent and clear in expression; unreflective means giving no serious thought to things. The pairing is the author's way of saying that fluency has replaced thought.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 raises cultural heritage, a theme absent from the passage.

 

• Option 3 overstates the case; the author criticises the loss of stillness, not formal education.

 

• Option 4 brings in economic consequences, which the passage never discusses.

 

NOTE

 

• The last sentence of an argumentative passage almost always carries the author's conclusion or warning. In SSC comprehension, one question from every such passage is usually built on it.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

She insisted on him to sign the document immediately.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. on his signing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "insist" takes the preposition "on", and a preposition is always followed by a gerund (V + ing), never by an infinitive (to + V1). So on him to sign is wrong.

 

• When a gerund has a subject of its own, that subject is put in the possessive case. The correct form is therefore "on his signing".

◦ Corrected sentence: She insisted on his signing the document immediately.
◦ Example: They objected to my leaving early.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "on him signing" uses the objective case; though heard in informal speech, SSC follows the traditional rule requiring the possessive before a gerund.

 

• Option 3: "that he signs" would need the subjunctive "that he sign" after insist, and in any case the preposition "on" must then be dropped.

 

• Option 4: "for him to signing" mixes an infinitive structure with a gerund and is grammatically impossible.

 

NOTE

 

• Other verbs and phrases followed by preposition + gerund: object to, look forward to, be accustomed to, with a view to, succeed in, refrain from, prevent from, think of, insist on. Note especially that in these, "to" is a preposition, so looking forward to meeting you is correct.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The manual explains how to install the software, how to configure it and the troubleshooting of common errors.
option_3: and to troubleshoot of common errors
option_4: and how to troubleshoot common errors
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. and how to troubleshoot common errors.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is one of parallelism (parallel structure) — items joined in a series must share the same grammatical form.

 

• The first two items are infinitive phrases introduced by "how to": how to install … how to configure … The third item must follow the same pattern: how to troubleshoot. A noun phrase ("the troubleshooting of") breaks the series.

◦ Corrected sentence: The manual explains how to install the software, how to configure it and how to troubleshoot common errors.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is still a noun phrase ("troubleshooting for") and therefore not parallel with the earlier infinitives.

 

• Option 2 is an awkward noun cluster and also breaks the pattern.

 

• Option 3 wrongly inserts the preposition "of" after the infinitive; to troubleshoot takes a direct object, not "of".

 

NOTE

 

• Parallelism is tested repeatedly in SSC. Keep the forms uniform: verb + verb (She likes reading, writing and painting), noun + noun, infinitive + infinitive. It applies with special force after not only … but also, either … or, both … and.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

The teacher said to the students, "Do not waste your time on trivial disputes."
option_1: The teacher said the students that they do not waste their time on trivial disputes.
option_2: The teacher told the students to not wasting their time on trivial disputes.
option_3: The teacher advised the students not to waste their time on trivial disputes.
option_4: The teacher advised the students that do not waste your time on trivial disputes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The teacher advised the students not to waste their time on trivial disputes.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported sentence is a negative imperative (an order or piece of advice beginning with "Do not"). Its rules of conversion are:

◦ The reporting verb said to changes to advised / told / ordered / requested, according to the sense.
◦ The conjunction "that" is dropped.
◦ The imperative becomes "not to + V1".
◦ Pronouns change according to the subject — here "your" → "their".

 

• Applying these: "Do not waste your time…" → advised the students not to waste their time…

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 retains "that" with an imperative and also uses the wrong structure "said the students" instead of "said to the students" or "told the students".

 

• Option 2 uses "to not wasting", which is grammatically impossible — after to the base form is required.

 

• Option 4 keeps the sentence in the direct form ("do not waste your time") inside a that-clause, which is not indirect speech at all.

 

NOTE

 

• Imperative conversions to remember: Order → ordered/commanded + to; Request → requested + to; Advice → advised + to; Negative imperative → forbade + to or told … not to.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

She exclaimed with delight that it was a wonderful performance.
option_1: "It was a wonderful performance," she said with delight.
option_2: "How wonderful performance it is!" she exclaimed with delight.
option_3: "That is a wonderful performance," she exclaimed with delight.
option_4: "What a wonderful performance!" she exclaimed with delight.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. "What a wonderful performance!" she exclaimed with delight.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrase "exclaimed with delight" signals that the original sentence was exclamatory. In converting back to direct speech:

◦ The that-clause is turned into an exclamatory sentence ending with an exclamation mark (!).
◦ The past tense "was" is restored to the present (understood) form used at the moment of speaking.
◦ The words are enclosed in inverted commas and the reporting verb is retained.

 

• "What" is used before a noun or noun phrase — What a wonderful performance! This is why Option 4 is correct.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses the neutral reporting verb "said" and a full stop, losing the exclamatory force entirely.

 

• Option 2 misuses "How", which must be followed by an adjective or adverb, not a noun phrase — the correct form would be How wonderful the performance is!

 

• Option 3 is a plain assertive sentence and does not match "exclaimed".

 

NOTE

 

• Remember the rule: "What a/an + adjective + noun!" but "How + adjective/adverb + subject + verb!"

 

• Common exclamatory reporting verbs: exclaimed with joy/sorrow/wonder/regret, cried out, wished (for "May…!").

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. For decades the old stepwell at the edge of the village lay choked with silt and refuse.

 

A. Encouraged by the change, the panchayat fenced the site and planted trees around it.

 

B. A group of students, home for the summer, decided to clear it as a vacation project.

 

C. Within weeks the water table rose and the wells in the neighbouring fields began to yield again.

 

D. What had begun as a holiday task had quietly restored the village's oldest source of water.

 

S2. Today the stepwell supplies three hamlets through the driest months of the year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. B-C-A-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – C – A – D – S2. The paragraph follows a clear problem → action → result → consolidation → conclusion order.

 

• S1 states the problem — the stepwell lay choked for decades.

◦ B supplies the action: the students "decided to clear it", and the pronoun it refers directly back to the stepwell in S1.
◦ C gives the immediate result of that action — the water table rose.
◦ A begins with "Encouraged by the change", and "the change" can only mean the rise in the water table described in C. So A must follow C.
◦ D is a summing-up sentence ("What had begun as a holiday task …") that looks back over the whole episode and leads naturally into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (C-B-D-A) places the result before the action, which is illogical.

 

• Option 3 (B-D-C-A) puts the concluding sentence D in the middle of the narrative.

 

• Option 4 (D-B-A-C) opens with the conclusion and leaves "the change" in A unexplained.

 

NOTE

 

• In rearrangement questions, hunt for linking devices: pronouns (it, they, this), demonstratives (the change, such a step), and connectives (however, therefore, encouraged by). Each one binds a sentence to the one immediately before it.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. Handwriting was once regarded as a reliable index of a person's character.

 

A. Employers, matrimonial agencies and even some courts consulted graphologists with complete confidence.

 

B. Controlled studies repeatedly failed to establish any link between the shape of letters and the traits they supposedly revealed.

 

C. The claim, however, did not survive serious scientific scrutiny.

 

D. What had long passed for insight turned out to be little more than confident guesswork.

 

S2. Graphology now survives largely as a parlour amusement rather than a professional tool.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. A-C-B-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – A – C – B – D – S2. The paragraph moves from belief → evidence of that belief → challenge → proof → verdict.

 

• S1 introduces the old belief that handwriting revealed character.

◦ A illustrates how widely that belief was trusted — employers, agencies and courts consulted graphologists. It expands S1 and must come immediately after it.
◦ C introduces the turn in the argument with the contrast marker "however", and "The claim" refers back to the belief stated in S1 and A.
◦ B supplies the evidence for C — the controlled studies that found no link.
◦ D delivers the verdict ("little more than confident guesswork"), which leads directly to the present-day position in S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (C-A-B-D) places the contrast "however" before the belief has been fully established, so A is left stranded after the rebuttal.

 

• Option 2 (A-B-C-D) gives the evidence before the claim is challenged, leaving "however" in C without a preceding statement to contrast with.

 

• Option 4 (C-B-A-D) wrongly puts A, which supports the old belief, after the belief has already been demolished.

 

NOTE

 

• A sentence beginning with "however", "but", "on the contrary" or "nevertheless" can never be the first of the jumbled set — it must follow the idea it contradicts. This single test eliminates two options here at once.
